title: Two deaths
hookLine: Sariputta goes home to teach his mother and dies; Moggallana is killed by bandits; the assembly seems empty (SN 47.14)
last: A MIND LIKE THE EARTH, WITHOUT ILL WILL.

cards: A young novice named Cunda is walking to Savatthi with something that isn't his: a bowl and a robe. They belonged to Sariputta, his teacher.

In the Samyutta Nikaya, Sariputta has fallen gravely ill in a village in Magadha, and with that illness he has passed away. Cunda carries the bowl and robe to Ananda, and Ananda brings him to the Buddha.
That's how the news arrives: not with a speech, but with a monk's few belongings, carried by hand. Two friends once made a pact. Today, the texts let them go.

teach.b: First, Sariputta. The discourse says only that he was sick in a village of Magadha and died there.

Later commentaries add a story. Tradition says he went back to the house where he was born, because his mother had never accepted the Buddha's teaching, and that in his last night he taught her and she understood.
A son's last work, done at home. Second, Moggallana. Here too the discourses say little.
A later story in the commentaries tells that he was attacked by bandits, hired by rivals of the Buddha's community, and killed. Tradition adds that he could have escaped, and in the end let it come.
Third, the empty assembly. Not long after both had died, the Buddha is sitting in the open air at Ukkacela, on the bank of the Ganges, with a crowd of monks around him. He looks over them in silence.
Then he says, in paraphrase: this assembly seems empty to me now. When those two were alive, it was not empty. Wherever they were staying, I had no worry about that place.
Fourth, the tree. The Buddha goes on: how could anything that's born, made, bound to break, not break?
It's as if the largest branches had fallen from a great tree that still stands, sound at the heart.
The tree goes on. The branches are gone. And then the words heard earlier on this path: be islands to yourselves, with the dhamma as your refuge.
Look back at the pair: a festival gone hollow, a pact, a verse passed on, the general, the powers, the earth, and today, two deaths.

how: Relics said to be those of Sariputta and Moggallana are honored at some Buddhist sites, and the two disciples are remembered together in temples and at Buddhist festivals.

o: two monks who died guarding the relics
the passing of the Buddha's mother and father
how Sariputta and Moggallana each passed away

s: the Buddha said the assembly seemed empty without the two
he looked over a full crowd of monks and said so.
the discourses describe Moggallana's death in detail
the bandits come from a later story in the commentaries.
the Buddha compared the loss to a tree falling down
the tree still stands; its largest branches have fallen.

games.q: you're Cunda, the novice who looked after Sariputta. he has died of his illness. what do you do with his bowl and robe?
o: keep them as a memory of your teacher.
carry them to Ananda and the Buddha.
games.why: he carries them all the way to Savatthi, to Ananda, who brings him to the Buddha. the news arrives as a bowl and a robe.

practice: Bring to mind two people who have been something like those two for you, one who helped you understand and one who helped you keep going, living or gone, and let each face come clearly.
Notice how a room feels with them in it, and silently thank each one by name.

wordCard.voice: Two deaths. Sariputta dies of illness; a later story says Moggallana was killed by bandits; and the Buddha says the assembly seems empty without them. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: final nibbana, the word the texts use for the death of an awakened one.

carryVoice: Your line: the assembly seems empty. The great tree still stands, though its largest branches are gone. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Commentarial tradition (Sariputta's last night with his mother; Moggallana and the bandits, e.g. the Dhammapada commentary on verses 137–140)
